title: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computer Revealed

segments.label: Cold Open – The Teaser
segments.text: What if a rusted lump from a sunken ship was actually an ancient computer? In this video we’ll reveal why that crazy idea is true and how a 2nd‑century BC Greek device could predict eclipses and the movements of the heavens decades in advance. You’ll see the shocking discovery that the Antikythera mechanism isn’t a mysterious relic but the world’s oldest analogue computer, built with dozens of interlocking bronze gears that mimic the motions of the Moon and Sun. Picture pulling a green‑tinged chunk of bronze and wood from the deep, opening it like a forgotten pocket watch, and finding a complex celestial clock that models the Moon’s speeding perigee – a trick first described by Hipparchus. Stay with us and we’ll walk through the X‑ray scans that exposed 35 meshing gears, the wooden case that protected them, and the inscriptions that unlock ancient Olympic cycles. By the end you’ll understand how this single artifact rewrote our view of ancient technology and why it still amazes scientists today.

segments.label: Discovery – From Wreck to Museum
segments.text: Ever wonder how a rusted lump from the sea became a star exhibit? In early 1900, Captain Dimitrios Kontos and his sponge‑diver crew from Symi hauled up a Roman cargo wreck at 45 m depth off Antikythera. They pulled up statues, glass, coins—and a mysterious bronze‑wood block. You can picture the divers hauling a 34 cm by 18 cm case, its bronze turned green by seawater. The treasure trove was shipped straight to Athens’ National Archaeological Museum. Two years passed while curators polished marble and polished bronze. Then, on 17 May 1902, archaeologist Valerios Stais, with his cousin politician Spyridon Stais, spotted a gear wheel embedded in the corroded piece. He thought it might be an astronomical clock. That single gear sparked the first study of the object. The mechanism eventually split into three major chunks, later catalogued as 82 fragments. Four of those fragments still hold gears, the largest about 13 cm across with 223 teeth. All pieces now sit in the museum alongside detailed reconstructions. Curious how those fragments were reassembled? We’ll see how scholars teased the bronze brain apart in the next reveal.

segments.label: Design & Mechanics – Inside the Bronze Brain
segments.text: Inside the bronze case, thirty‑five bronze gears interlock like a tiny machine city. Thirty of those gears still peek out from the surviving fragments. The biggest wheel spans about 13 cm, its rim crowded with 223 teeth. Imagine you turning that hand crank and feeling the whole constellation shift. The crank connects to a crown gear that drives the largest wheel. One turn spins the date pointer and nudges every other gear at once. This cascade powers dials that trace the Sun’s path across the zodiac. You can picture the Moon’s wobble captured by epicyclic gears inside. Those epicyclic teeth accelerate the Moon when it nears perigee and slow it near apogee. How could such precise astronomy fit in a hand‑held box? The answer lies in the clever gear ratios, each tooth count tuned to celestial cycles. So when you twist the crank, the mechanism simultaneously predicts eclipses, lunar phases, and solar positions. Every gear teeth meshes perfectly, turning the bronze brain into an ancient analog computer. Stay tuned, because the next reveal shows how scientists peeled back the rust to read its secrets.

segments.label: Functions – Calendars, Eclipses, and Games
segments.text: You’ve probably seen that weird bronze clock with two rings. The front ring stays still, marked with the twelve zodiac signs. The outer ring spins, showing the Egyptian calendar – twelve months of thirty days plus five extra days. Turn the crank and the calendar ring slides against the zodiac, lining dates with the stars. How does it handle longer cycles? On the back, three dials spin: a 19‑year Metonic cycle, an 18‑year Saros eclipse cycle, and a four‑year games cycle like the ancient Olympiad. Each full turn moves tiny pointers over engraved numbers. Ever wonder how the Moon’s face changes? A half‑black, half‑white ball on a differential gear spins, displaying the real‑time lunar phase. The mechanism even carries numbers for Venus and Saturn’s synodic periods, hinting at planetary forecasts. Picture the gears clicking, each tooth advancing a calendar, an eclipse, a game, or a planet’s return. What mystery still hides in those bronze gears? The next reveal will show how scientists stripped away rust to read the hidden planetary calculations.

segments.label: Scientific Investigation – Uncovering the Secrets
segments.text: What did they see when they sliced through centuries of rust? In 2005 a Cardiff University team, led by Mike Edmunds, pointed an X‑ray scanner at the bronze brain. The machine buzzed, sending high‑resolution X‑rays through each fragment. Images popped up, revealing tiny teeth and faint letters hidden beneath the corroded shell. You could actually count the gears – thirty‑five meshing bronze wheels, though only thirty still show up in the scans. The biggest gear is about 13 cm across and has 223 teeth. Did you ever wonder how the ancients could model the Moon’s wobble? The scans uncovered a gear train that mimics the Moon’s irregular orbit – faster at perigee, slower at apogee – the exact pattern Hipparchus of Rhodes studied in the 2nd century BC. The X‑ray images also exposed ghostly inscriptions that once covered the outer casing. Those numbers link to the synodic cycles of Venus and Saturn, a link confirmed in 2016. So the rust wasn’t a barrier; it was a veil that the X‑ray peeled away, exposing the mechanism’s true complexity. What hidden part might still be missing, waiting for the next breakthrough?

segments.label: Payoff – Legacy and Mystery
segments.text: What does a bronze brain from 200 BC mean for you? It tells you the Antikythera mechanism predates its 70‑60 BC shipwreck by decades. Some scholars calibrate it to 23 December 178 BC; others argue for 204 BC. You’re looking at gearwork that out‑classed anything for roughly 1,500 years until 14th‑century European clocks appeared. How could such complexity arise so early? The design links to Hellenistic astronomers like Hipparchus and perhaps Archimedes’ school. Picture a wooden case about 34 cm × 18 cm × 9 cm, a 13 cm gear with 223 teeth, all hand‑crafted. Does this change your idea of ancient engineering? Yes—it proves analog computation existed millennia before modern computers. The device could predict eclipses and Olympic cycles decades ahead. It was discovered in 1901 among wreckage off Antikythera and split into 82 fragments, four of which hold gears. The largest gear measured about 13 cm in diameter. Researchers in 2022 suggested the initial calibration date, not construction date, could be 23 December 178 BC; other experts favor 204 BC.
